candidates.source_title: Weapons and dogs seized, stolen machinery recovered from farm - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_summary: A 53-year-old man was arrested, seven dogs seized and suspected stolen farm machinery worth around £30,000 recovered after police executed a warrant at a farm in Rochdale.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: A 53-year-old man was arrested, seven dogs seized and suspected stolen farm machinery worth around £30,000 has been recovered after police executed a warrant at a farm in Rochdale. They recovered about £30,000 worth of suspected stolen farm and building machinery, a machete and four other suspected offensive weapons and seven dogs have been seized following a warrant at the rural property. The activity was carried out as part of ongoing work to tackle rural crime during National Rural Crime Week, which highlights the impact offences such as machinery theft can have on rural communities and businesses. Officers from the Rochdale Neighbourhood Policing Team, supported by Dog Liaison Officers, the National Construction and Agricultural Theft Team (NCATT) and drone units, executed a warrant at around 9am today as part of an investigation into stolen farm and building machinery. A 53-year-old man was arrested. Image: GMP During searches of the property, officers seized suspected stolen farm and building machinery, including a tractor, an agricultural trailer and other farming equipment. A 53-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of handling stolen goods, possessing an offensive weapon in a private dwelling and breaching a court order prohibiting him from keeping dogs. Inspector Clem Jones, of the Rochdale Neighbourhood Policing Team, said: “Today’s warrant serves as a reminder that rural crime will not be tolerated. It is an often-overlooked issue that can have a significant impact on communities and the livelihoods of those who live and work in the countryside.

candidates.source_summary: More than 350 staff at four Greater Manchester hospitals are due to walk out later this month.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Salford Royal Hospital is one of four Manchester sites affected More than 350 staff at four Greater Manchester hospitals are set to strike again in an ongoing row about overtime payments. Unison said talks had stalled and claimed the Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust had rejected offers to resume negotiations. The workers, including operating theatre staff at Salford Royal Hospital, Royal Oldham Hospital, Rochdale Infirmary and Fairfield Hospital in Bury, will strike on 14, 15 and 17 September. The latest action follows previous strikes in June and August. The trust said it would do "everything it can to minimise the impact on patients and maintain high standards of care and quality at all times." The dispute centres on the use of NHS Professionals to manage overtime. Unison said staff could earn less for some overtime shifts than they would on a normal shift, with some workers missing out on as much as Â£80. The union's North West regional organiser Kevin Dolan said the trust had given "no indication that it's willing to re-enter negotiations".

candidates.source_title: Rochdale signals Middleton intent with plan to buy Warwick Mill - Place North West
candidates.source_summary: The council has signed an option agreement with the owner of the long-vacant former cotton mill in an effort to set a positive tone for the regeneration of the town. Developer Capital&Centric is in pole position to redevelop the grade two-listed asset into apartments.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Warwick Mill is a symbol of Middleton's decline, according to the co-chair of the town's MDC. Credit: via Rochdale Council The council has signed an option agreement with the owner of the long-vacant former cotton mill in an effort to set a positive tone for the regeneration of the town. Developer Capital&Centric is in pole position to redevelop the grade two-listed asset into apartments. Sitting at the heart of the town’s 200-acre Mayoral Development Zone and built in 1907, Warwick Mill is set to be the first major project to come forward in the town’s planned regeneration following talks between the current owner – Hong Kong-based Kam Lei Fong – Rochdale Council, the town’s Mayoral Development Corporation, and the in-vogue developer. Actor Steve Coogan, co-chair of the Middleton MDC, told Place North West the mill is an obvious place to start turning Middleton’s fortunes around. “It happens to be a factory that is visible from almost every part of Middleton. It’s looming over it,” said Coogan, who grew up in Middleton. “I think it was [Prime Minister] Andy [Burnham] who said ‘do that first’.” At present, the massive red brick building on Oldham Road is in a sorry state. It ceased operations as a mill in the 1960s and has only been used sporadically since. Its many windows are either boarded up or smashed. Rose Marley, co-chair of Middleton MDC and chief executive of Co-operatives UK, said Warwick Mill has become “symbolic of decay, post-industrialised distress, a lack of skills, [and] a lack of hope”.

candidates.source_title: East Lancashire Railway welcomes its first female steam locomotive driver
candidates.source_summary: The East Lancashire Railway has its first female steam locomotive driver after Steph Elwood successfully completed her driving assessments.
candidates.source_body_excerpt:
She progressed through the railway's steam department from cleaner to fireman before qualifying to drive steam locomotives.

Steph is now officially a Passed Fireman, allowing her to carry out both firing and driving turns on the heritage railway.

She said her interest in heritage railways began when she attended her first Santa Special at two months old.

Steph said: “I’m so pleased to be able to say that I’ve now successfully passed all my driving assessments to become the first female steam train driver at the East Lancashire Railway. It feels like such a huge achievement, and I still can’t quite believe that I’m now officially a Passed Fireman, allowing me to carry out both firing and driving turns.

“My love of heritage railways goes back to when I was just two months old, when I attended my first Santa Special. To think that, all these years later, I would be here achieving this is something I could never have imagined. From being a little girl fascinated by steam trains to now having the opportunity to drive one myself is a dream come true.

“I’m incredibly grateful to everyone who has supported, encouraged and helped me along the way. There have been challenges and a lot to learn, but every step of the journey has made reaching this moment even more rewarding.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Ofsted inspectors have highlighted the personal development and wellbeing of students, as well as attendance and behaviour at Cardinal Langley RC High School. The Middleton high school also met the expected standards for achievement, curriculum and teaching, inclusion, leadership and governance and post-16 provision as inspectors recognised that “pupils are proud of their school . . . and enjoy their learning”. The report by lead inspector Richard Wakefield, follows the inspectors’ visit on June 9 and returning 9 July 9. Receiving a strong standard for attendance and behaviour, the inspectors said: “Pupils’ overall attendance, including disadvantaged pupils and those with special educational needs and/or disabilities, has consistently improved and is significantly above the national average. “Leaders create a calm and caring environment where positive behaviour is expected. Pupils are polite and respectful in lessons and at social times. “They cooperate well with each other and build supportive relationships with staff. Pupils are not allowed to use mobile phones in school and have begun to develop other interests together, such as playing board games. This is developing their communication skills. Year 12 students visit Lancaster University as part of their Next Steps week. Image: Cardinal Langley “Leaders monitor unwanted behaviours, such as bullying. Pupils know that these behaviours are not tolerated. Staff deal quickly and effectively with any issues that do arise. Leaders provide proactive support for a small minority of pupils who need help to improve their behaviour.”

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Gillingham celebrated their first win of the season with a comfortable 4-1 victory at 10-man Rochdale in Sky Bet League Two. Despite losing both Zech Obiero, who was carried off on a stretcher, and Will Goodwin early on, the visitors took the lead in the 32nd minute when James Brophy curled a shot wide of Nils Ramming. Omar Beckles doubled the lead in the 53rd minute, pouncing on a loose ball six yards from goal – and the home side capitulated thereafter. Three minutes later Lamin Sillah effectively wrapped up the three points. Eli King’s delivery was nodded down by Andy Smith and Sillah headed home. Dale were reduced to 10 men when Ed Francis saw red for a second bookable offence on the hour mark. Gills stopper Oliver Wright made a fine double save to deny Mani Dieseruvwe and Luke Hannant before Brophy scored a superb fourth. Midway through the second half Brophy drifted in from the left and dribbled the ball round four defenders before beating Ramming from close range. Dale debutant Charlie Tasker headed an 87th minute reply for the home side.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Visitors have been enjoying freshly made cuppas and homemade treats ahead of the formal opening of Denehurst Park café this weekend — and can’t wait to come back for more. The café, on the ground floor of the 19th century manor house in Rochdale, is being run by local Community Interest Company Get Together After Serving (GTAS). Staffed entirely by former armed forces personnel and their families, the café has been welcoming visitors all week ahead of the official opening today. Set up by Rochdale residents Adam Trennery, Wayne Traynor and Wayne Simms, GTAS aims to support the local veteran community in a number of ways, including through wellbeing programmes and local events and get-togethers. Customers can expect café favourites like hot and cold sandwiches, cakes, breakfasts and tea and coffee. candidates.source_body_excerpt: A 19th Century manor house in Rochdale has been transformed into a café, run solely by ex-military personnel. Denehurst House, right in the heart of Denehurst Park, will officially open its doors tomorrow (Saturday, September 5). The new venue will be managed and run by Get Together After Serving (GTAS) and staffed entirely by former armed forces personnel and their families. Café favourites such as hot and cold sandwiches, cakes, breakfasts and tea and coffee will all be on offer. rochdale -council>Rochdale council says that customers can expect ‘generous opening hours’ and ‘honest’ prices. With plenty of space, the café will also serve as a spot where local veterans can get together. Denehurst House’s revamp, commissioned by Rochdale council, includes five flats for veterans on the above floors as well as the remodelling of the ground floor for the café. Local veteran, Adam Trennery, who is one of the directors at GTAS, said: “We’re made up to have the opportunity to open a café in this brilliant space. The house and its grounds were donated to the town in 1932 and were later used as council offices, before being left empty for a number of years. candidates.source_title: 'Something dangerous' fed to Rochdale horse by campers, owner says - ManchesterWorld
candidates.source_summary: Julie Kershaw, 58, was left 'upset and stressed' after campers fed her 13-year-old horse Frank something that left him in a critical condition, with a vet bill of £235 and extra costs for food.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: A horrified horse owner found her beloved pet trembling helplessly on the ground and close to death after he was fed dangerous scraps by campers. Julie Kershaw, 58, raced to the field where she keeps 13-year-old Frank to find him shaking uncontrollably, barely able to walk and battling a potentially fatal infection. As he lay stricken on the grass in Rochdale, Gtr Manchester., the terrified owner feared Frank would not survive the night - as she said she believes campers fed him human food. Julie said: "With the state he was in, I didn't think he was going to be alive in the morning. "He was really shaking and couldn't walk." Julie does not know exactly what Frank ate, but is convinced he was fed something dangerous by visitors because he has lived safely in the same field throughout his life. Frank had been discovered in distress by 13-year-old Freya and her mum Rachel while they were out walking. They saw the horse suddenly collapse, roll onto his side and begin breathing heavily as his whole body shook. Freya remained beside him and offered comfort while Rachel issued a frantic Facebook appeal to find his owner. Julie had been out all day when her daughter, who was on the phone to a friend, alerted her to the drama. The bistro worker, who lives around 15 minutes away from the field, immediately realised the stricken animal was Frank. She said: "I must have had 20 phone calls and it was all over Facebook." Julie and others managed to get Frank into a stable before a vet arrived within 40 minutes. He needed four injections during an emergency visit which continued until around 10.30pm. Julie said: "They told us it was colitis and said it was an infection in the colon. He was in a critical condition. "It's just so scary - people don't realise how dangerous it is to feed horses." Julie was warned the inflammation could spread and prove fatal. Horse owners have previously discovered chicken bones, tomatoes, red onions and lemons dumped among the animals. In one incident, Julie said she spent weeks picking Brussels sprouts out of the field last Christmas when visitors threw them for horses. She said: "It keeps happening and it’s a nightmare. A horse is part of a family, so I was so upset and stressed. "The vet bill was £235, but we also had to spend on food - I spent about £300 in altogether. "It all happened because of people's ignorance. "Everyone has a phone - so why can't they just search what you can and can't feed a horse?" Julie said the situation has worsened since walkers discovered the previously quiet spot during the pandemic. Fellow horse owner Patsy said visitors had even been spotted standing beside the animals carrying a chicken kebab and naan bread. Julie warned that even conventional treats such as apples and carrots can become dangerous if dozens of visitors each feed them to the horses.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Rochdale's avoidable deaths are rising as alcohol, drugs and smoking drive harm above national averages; a new council report sets out the response. Rochdale built the co-operative movement and much of the modern welfare argument; today the borough's hardest statistic is that more of its residents are dying from causes that treatment, prevention or a little more money could have avoided. A Tackling Addiction report presented to the town hall this week identifies the three drivers as alcohol, drugs and smoking, and concedes that avoidable deaths are rising even where consumption is not. The National Drug Treatment Monitoring System estimates that 2,905 people in Rochdale are dependent on alcohol and 1,831 use opiates or crack cocaine. Alcohol-related deaths run well above the national average, with a sharp spike in 2020 around the pandemic. Smoking tells the same story in slower motion. The rate has fallen but stands at 12.7%, against a national average of 10.9%, which equates to roughly 22,000 adult smokers. The report estimates Rochdale residents spend £66.2 million (about KES 11.6 billion) a year on tobacco, legal and illegal, and hospital admissions linked to smoking run above average. For treatment for drug and alcohol issues, increased outreach work and follow ups as well as working with different groups of people such as the homeless, women and over 50s.
